questions.question: For a real-valued function $f\colon\boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, what is $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$?
options: The matrix of second partial derivatives at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.
The scalar sum of the first partial derivatives at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.
The column vector of first partial derivatives at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.

questions.question: What condition on $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is included for the gradient?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is a boundary point of the set $\boldsymbol{E}$.

questions.question: For $f(x,y) = \mathrm{e}^{x+y}$, what is $\nabla f(x,y)$?
For $f(x,y) = x^2y+y^3$, what is $\nabla f(x,y)$?

Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$, and let $\boldsymbol{v}$ be a unit vector. What does $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\cdot\boldsymbol{v}$ represent in general?
options: The steepest rate of increase of $f$ at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.

questions.question: What is said when $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \boldsymbol{0}$?
options: Every directional derivative must be positive.

questions.question: Suppose $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}$. What is $\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$?
For $f(x,y) = x^2y+y^3$, what is $\nabla f(1,1)$?
Why does the definition require $f$ to be real-valued?
options: Because partial derivatives exist only for functions into $\mathbb{R}$.
Because only real-valued functions can be totally differentiable.
Because the gradient is the vector of partial derivatives of one scalar function.
Because a real-valued $f$ is guaranteed to have all of its first partial derivatives.

questions.question: If $\nabla f(x_0)\ne0$, which directional-derivative claim is justified?
options: The directional derivative is the same in every unit direction.
The directional derivative is largest in the gradient direction.
The gradient is tangent to the level set of $f$ through the point $x_0$.
The largest decrease of $f$ occurs in the gradient direction.

questions.question: If $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}3/5\\4/5\end{pmatrix}$, what is $\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$?
For $f(x,y) = \mathrm{e}^{x+y}$, at which point below is the gradient equal to $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$?
How many components does $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$ have for $f\colon E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$?
Which derivatives form the entries of the gradient?
options: The values of $f$ at all points.
The directional derivatives in every possible direction as separate entries.

questions.question: What does $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\boldsymbol{0}$ indicate in this terminology?
options: $f$ is not differentiable at any point of its domain.

questions.question: For $f(x,y)=x+y$, what is $\nabla f(x,y)$?
For $f(x,y)=x^2+3y$, what is $\nabla f(2,1)$?
If $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}$, what is $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ called?
options: A boundary point of the domain.

questions.question: What is the relation between the gradient and directional derivatives?
options: The norm of the gradient equals the directional derivative in every direction
Directional derivatives exist only along the gradient direction itself
The directional derivative is the product of $\|\nabla f\|$ and $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|$
The gradient dotted with a unit vector gives the directional derivative

questions.question: If $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}$, what is $\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$?
